sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
Mechanical systems are LTI when their elements are linear: springs (\(F = kx\)), viscous dampers (\(F = b\dot x\)) and masses (\(F = m\ddot x\)). Newton's law applied to each mass gives a constant-coefficient differential equation, just like a circuit.

A mass on a spring with a damper obeys \(m\ddot x + b\dot x + kx = F\). Its transfer function is \(1/(ms^2 + bs + k)\), with natural frequency \(\sqrt{k/m}\) and damping ratio \(b/(2\sqrt{km})\). A rotating shaft with inertia \(J\) and friction \(b\) is first order in speed, with time constant \(J/b\). Cruise control is a first-order model of car speed against drag.

Real mechanisms are only approximately linear: Coulomb friction, backlash and saturation break the model. Linearising around an operating point is the standard way to apply LTI tools to them.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\[ m\ddot x + b\dot x + kx = F, \qquad \omega_n = \sqrt{\frac km}, \qquad \zeta = \frac{b}{2\sqrt{km}} \]
\[ J\dot\omega + b\omega = \tau \;\Rightarrow\; \tau_m = J/b \]
sections.figure_alt: Shaft speed rising exponentially toward its final value after a torque step.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: A 3 kg mass on a 300 N/m spring with \(b = 18\ \mathrm{N\,s/m}\) has \(\omega_n = 10\ \mathrm{rad/s}\) and \(\zeta = 0.3\). A 60 N step force moves it to 0.2 m, overshooting by about 37% first. A flywheel with \(J = 0.6\) and \(b = 0.15\) has a 4 s time constant.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Using weight instead of mass.
- Getting the damper sign wrong in the free-body diagram.
- Applying LTI results to dry friction.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: The same models are the plants for the control loops of ME 132 and Feedback Systems.
